section.title: Submission to Governing Authorities
section.sectionRationale: From love within and beyond the church Paul turns to the believer's life under the state. Having just forbidden personal vengeance, he now teaches that God has ordained the governing authority to bear the sword as His servant for good and His avenger against wrongdoing. Submission to lawful authority, the payment of taxes, and the giving of honor are presented as a matter not merely of fear but of conscience before God.
section.thesis: Governing authority is instituted by God as His servant for the public good and His avenger against evil, so believers are to submit for conscience' sake and render what is owed, taxes, revenue, respect, and honor, all under the higher allegiance owed to God alone.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the divine institution of authority and the seriousness of resisting it; the ruler as God's servant for good and avenger of wrath; and the resulting duty to submit in conscience and to pay what is owed.

verses.text: Everyone must submit himself to the governing {{exousia|authorities}}, for there is no authority except that which is from God. The authorities that exist have been appointed by God.
Consequently, whoever resists authority is opposing what God has set in place, and those who do so will bring judgment on themselves.

units.label: The ruler as God's servant
units.note: an agent of retribution, not bearing the sword in vain

verses.text: For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad. Do you want to be unafraid of the one in authority? Then do what is right, and you will have his approval.

For he is God’s {{diakonos|servant}} for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, for he does not carry the {{machaira|sword}} in vain. He is God’s servant, an agent of retribution to the wrongdoer.

units.label: Submit and pay what is owed

verses.text: Therefore it is necessary to submit to authority, not only to avoid punishment, but also as a matter of conscience.
This is also why you pay taxes. For the authorities are God’s {{leitourgos|servants}}, who devote themselves to their work.
Pay everyone what you owe him: taxes to whom taxes are due, revenue to whom revenue is due, respect to whom respect is due, honor to whom honor is due.

exousia.gloss: Authority, the rightful power to govern. Paul says there is no exousia except from God; all legitimate authority is derived, held on loan from the God who is the source of all rule. This both dignifies the office and limits it, for the authority answers to the God who gave it.

diakonos.gloss: A servant, one who ministers on behalf of another. Remarkably, Paul calls the civil ruler God's diakonos, God's servant for your good. The governing authority, whether it knows it or not, serves the purposes of God by restraining evil and promoting order for the common good.

machaira.gloss: A sword, the instrument of judicial force. The ruler does not bear the machaira in vain: God has entrusted to the state the power of the sword to punish wrongdoing. This is the God-appointed answer to personal vengeance, which Paul has just forbidden, placing retribution in the hands of the ordained authority.

leitourgos.gloss: A minister or public servant, a word often used of priestly or official service. Paul calls the tax-collecting authorities God's leitourgoi, God's ministers who devote themselves to their work. The term dignifies civic office as a form of service under God, grounding the duty to pay taxes in God's own ordering of society.

basic.context: Paul has just told the church never to take personal revenge but to leave wrath to God. Now he shows one way God exercises that wrath in this present age: through the governing authority. Having addressed love within the church and toward enemies, he addresses the believer's life under the state. Government, he says, is not a necessary evil but a good ordained by God, His servant for the common good.
basic.hermeneutics: Read this in its place, right after the command to leave vengeance to God. The state is God's appointed means of restraining evil now, while final judgment waits. Paul speaks in general terms of authority as a divine institution; he is not blessing every act of every ruler, and the rest of Scripture makes clear that when the state commands what God forbids, we must obey God rather than men. Here the stress falls on the duty of submission.
basic.originalLanguages: There is no exousia, authority, except from God. The ruler is God's diakonos, His servant for our good, who does not bear the machaira, the sword, in vain. And the tax-gathering officials are God's leitourgoi, ministers who devote themselves to their work. Each word dignifies civil office as service under God.
basic.typology: The ordering of nations under God's rule runs back to His sovereignty over Pharaoh, Cyrus, and Nebuchadnezzar, all of whom served His purposes. The state's sword prefigures and serves the justice that belongs finally to God, and points forward to Christ, the King to whom all authority in heaven and earth has been given.
basic.christ: All earthly authority is derived from the God who has given all authority to the risen Christ. Jesus Himself submitted to Pilate's court, telling him he would have no power unless it were given from above. The Lord who taught us to render to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's is the true King over every ruler, and every throne will one day bow to Him.
basic.god: God is the source and Lord of all authority. He institutes rulers, works through them for good, and executes a measure of His justice through their office. The passage exalts God's sovereignty over human government, so that submission to lawful authority is ultimately submission to God's own ordering of the world, and the higher allegiance is always to Him.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Peter 2 likewise calls believers to submit to every human institution for the Lord's sake. Titus 3 urges obedience to rulers and readiness for good work. Daniel shows God ruling over kingdoms and setting up rulers. Acts 5 records the apostles insisting they must obey God rather than men.
basic.oneStory: God has always ruled over the nations, raising up and putting down kings to serve His purposes. He ordains government to restrain evil and uphold order until the day of final justice. That day comes with Christ, to whom all authority has been given and before whom every earthly power will bow, when the kingdom of the world becomes the kingdom of our Lord.

context.literary:
The paragraph is a tightly built argument, and its logic hangs on a series of 'for' clauses. Verse 1 gives the command, 'for' there is no authority except from God. Verse 3 explains why rulers are not to be feared by those doing right, 'for' rulers are not a terror to good conduct. Verse 4 says the ruler is God's servant, and verse 6 adds 'for' the authorities are God's servants. Each step answers the objection raised by the one before.

The passage is held together by a family of words about order. The command 'submit' (hypotasso) is built on the root tasso, to arrange or appoint. The authorities 'have been appointed' (tetagmenai) by God. Whoever 'resists' (antitasso) is opposing what God has 'set in place' (diatage). All four words come from the same root, so the sentence is a play on ordering: be ordered under the One who has ordered everything.

Structurally, verses 1 and 2 set the principle with a warning, verses 3 and 4 give the reason in terms of the ruler's function, and verses 5 to 7 draw out the duty. The paragraph is also lodged between two passages about love. It follows the ban on revenge in 12:19, and it is followed by the debt of love in 13:8. Many scholars note that 13:1-7 could be lifted out without interrupting the sense, but the reading adopted here, and the stronger one, is that the placement is intentional: the ruler's sword is the answer to the question left open by 'leave room for God's wrath'.
context.historical:
The Rome of about AD 57 was ruled by Nero, then a teenage emperor guided by Seneca and the prefect Burrus. The first five years of his reign were later remembered as a time of relative moderation. The empire gave its subjects the Pax Romana, safe roads and sea lanes, and courts that, while unequal, usually functioned. Paul himself would later appeal to Caesar's court and be heard, Acts 25:11, and had earlier been protected by Roman law in several cities, Acts 16:37-39, 18:12-17.

The tax question was especially live. Direct taxes (phoros) were levied on property and persons in the provinces, and indirect taxes (telos) were collected as customs on goods, often through private contractors who were notorious for extortion. The Roman historian Tacitus reports that in the late 50s the complaints against these collectors became so loud that the emperor considered abolishing the indirect taxes. Jewish Christians knew the history of tax revolts against Rome, and a political church could easily be thought to be a subversive one.

Paul's readers also knew that the state could be hostile. The believers in Rome had lived under the expulsion edict of Claudius, and Paul himself had been beaten and jailed by officials. The apostle is therefore not naive. He is writing to people who knew what the sword could do, and he gives them a theology in which the sword is not outside God's rule, even when it is abused. Jesus had told them to give to Caesar what is Caesar's, Matthew 22:21, and Jeremiah had told exiles in Babylon to seek the welfare of the city where they lived, Jeremiah 29:7.
context.canonical:
The teaching that rulers hold power under God runs through the Old Testament. Proverbs 8:15-16 says kings reign by wisdom, and Daniel tells the Babylonian king that the God of heaven gives the kingdom, 2:37-38, and that the Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom He wills, 4:17. Isaiah names the pagan Cyrus as the Lord's anointed, Isaiah 45:1, and Jeremiah calls Nebuchadnezzar God's servant, Jeremiah 25:9. Paul applies that long tradition to the present empire.

The New Testament repeats the teaching in a number of places. Peter tells believers to submit to every human institution for the Lord's sake, 1 Peter 2:13-17, and Titus is to remind his people to be subject to rulers, Titus 3:1. Timothy is told to pray for kings and all in authority, 1 Timothy 2:1-2. Jesus Himself told Pilate that he would have no authority unless it were given from above, John 19:11.

But the canon also records a boundary. The Hebrew midwives disobeyed Pharaoh's command, Exodus 1:15-21; Daniel's friends refused the golden image, Daniel 3, and Daniel kept praying, Daniel 6; and the apostles told the council that they must obey God rather than men, Acts 5:29. Revelation 13 pictures the state as a beast that demands worship and wages war on the saints. Romans 13 must therefore be read as one voice in a chorus: the state is God's servant, and a state that claims God's place has stopped being what Paul describes.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul's first aim was to keep the church out of needless trouble. A band of believers with a Jewish heritage in Rome could easily have been suspected of sedition, and he wanted their lives to answer the charge. 'Do what is right, and you will have his approval' is a pastoral expectation that good citizenship would, in ordinary conditions, count in their favour.

His deeper aim was theological. He wanted them to see the state under God, neither an idol nor a demon. If the ruler is God's servant, then the believer need not fear the empire as an ultimate power, nor worship it. The state is a creature with a job. The sentence 'there is no authority except that which is from God' undermines the claim of any emperor to be the source of his own power.

Third, Paul meant to teach them how to handle wrongs. Having told them not to avenge themselves, he points to where justice does lie in the present age. The conscience is engaged, because submission is not merely prudent: the believer obeys 'as a matter of conscience', knowing that to honour the office is to honour God who established it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The paragraph prescribes. Submit, pay taxes, give respect and honour. These are plain commands. What it describes is the ordinary purpose of government: to reward good and punish evil. It is not a verdict on any particular ruler, and it does not say that a government which has stopped doing that job must be obeyed in everything it demands.

The text addresses people who had no vote and no way to change the government. It speaks to the church as subjects, not as citizens of a democracy. Many readers therefore ask what changes where believers have a voice. The answer is that the principles of honour, lawful conduct, prayer and the payment of what is owed continue, while the opportunities to petition, vote, and speak, which Paul's readers lacked, are now additional ways of seeking the good of the city, Jeremiah 29:7. The passage also should not be used to silence the oppressed or to bless injustice. It is never found in the Bible as a weapon against the weak, and the prophets show God's anger at rulers who abuse their office.

debates.question: Does this passage command unconditional obedience to every government?

views.label: Submission that is real but not absolute
views.case: The historic reading takes Paul to command genuine submission to lawful authority as God's institution, while the wider witness of Scripture, we must obey God rather than men, sets a limit: when the state commands what God forbids, believers must obey God, though ready to bear the consequences.

views.label: Absolute, unconditional obedience
views.case: A minority have read the commands as allowing no exception, urging obedience to rulers in all things; but this collides with Acts 5, Daniel, and Revelation, and is not the mainstream Christian position.

debates.bearing: The orthodox reading honors the state as God's good ordinance and calls for real submission, while preserving the higher allegiance to God; Paul stresses the duty of submission here without cancelling the rest of Scripture's teaching on its limits.

debates.question: What is the sword the ruler bears in verse 4?

views.label: The judicial power to punish
views.case: The historic reading sees the sword as the state's God-given authority to enforce justice and punish wrongdoing, the appointed alternative to the personal vengeance forbidden in chapter 12.

views.label: Merely a symbol of office
views.case: Some soften it to a symbol of authority alone; but the context of retribution and being afraid points to real coercive power entrusted to the state.

debates.bearing: The sword signifies genuine, God-authorized force to restrain and punish evil, which is why the believer can renounce private revenge and trust God's ordained justice through the magistrate.

debates.question: Who are the 'authorities' (exousiai) in verse 1?

views.label: Human civil rulers
views.case: The context of taxes, the sword and the courts points to Roman officials, and Peter's parallel in 1 Peter 2:13-14 names the king and governors. This is the reading of the church from the earliest centuries and of the Reformers.

views.label: Rulers together with unseen powers behind them
views.case: In other letters Paul uses the same word for spiritual powers, Ephesians 6:12 and Colossians 2:15, and some have argued that he means both the visible officials and the powers standing behind them. The difficulty is that Paul speaks of people who carry swords, collect taxes and are to be paid honour, which fits human officials.

debates.bearing: The weight lies on human governors. Even if unseen powers stand behind them, the passage is about how believers conduct themselves toward the visible institutions of society.

study.originalLanguages:
The command 'submit' is hypotasso, to arrange oneself under. It is a middle or passive imperative in the Greek and does not mean to obey blindly. Paul uses the same verb for wives in Ephesians 5:22 and for believers in relation to one another in Ephesians 5:21, and Christ is said to be 'subjected' to the Father in 1 Corinthians 15:28. It is a posture of acknowledging an order, and it is different from the word for obey, hypakouo, which Paul chose not to use here. The difference matters: a person can be subject to an authority and still decline a particular command, as the apostles did before the council, accepting the penalty rather than rebelling.

The 'authorities' are exousiai, from the stem 'it is permitted', meaning the right or freedom to act. The word 'rulers' in verse 3 is archontes. Verse 1 begins 'every soul', pasa psyche, a Hebraism for 'everyone', which includes believers of every rank, even apostles.

The ruler is God's 'servant' in verse 4, diakonos, and again in verse 6 God's 'servants', leitourgoi. The first is the ordinary word for a helper or attendant, and the church uses it for its own ministers. The second is the word for a public servant or official, and in the Septuagint it was used for priests who served at the sanctuary. Using this temple word for tax collectors is a bold stroke: the humblest official stands in the line of those who serve God. The ruler is also 'an agent of retribution', ekdikos, 'avenger', related to the word for vengeance in 12:19, and the sword is machaira, the short sword carried as a sign of the right to punish. 'Wrath' is orge, and the tension is close between the ruler's wrath here and God's wrath in 12:19: the first is the instrument of the second.

The paragraph ends with two kinds of taxes, phoros and telos, the direct tribute and the customs duty, and two attitudes, phobos, usually 'fear' and here translated 'respect', and time, 'honour'. The ordinary word for fear appears in verses 3 and 4 too, which shows the range: reverence for those who bear the office, and fear of those who punish wrongdoing.

'Conscience', syneidesis, in verse 5 is the faculty by which a person knows with himself what he has done. Paul used it for the law written on Gentile hearts in 2:15, and for the reason behind obedience that goes deeper than fear of a penalty.

typology.type: Cyrus and Nebuchadnezzar as God's instruments, Isaiah 45:1 and Jeremiah 25:9
typology.fulfillment: God called a Persian king His anointed, Isaiah 45:1, and a Babylonian king His servant, Jeremiah 25:9, though neither knew Him. Their authority was real, and it served purposes they did not grasp. Romans 13 applies this pattern to Rome: even an unbelieving ruler, as ruler, is God's servant. In Christ the pattern reaches its centre. Pilate and Herod did what God's hand and plan had predestined to take place, Acts 4:27-28, yet without cancelling their guilt. The type falls short in that these kings were instruments; the Lord Jesus is the true King and the Son.

typology.type: The king under the law, Deuteronomy 17:14-20
typology.fulfillment: Israel's king was to write out a copy of the law, read it, and not exalt himself above his brothers. His office was an office under God. The ruler of Romans 13 is likewise a servant, not a source. The picture finds its end in the Son of David, who rules in righteousness, Isaiah 11:1-5, and to whom the Father has given all authority, Matthew 28:18. Every earthly ruler is measured against Him, and His reign is the standard by which the ruler's 'good' is finally defined. Israel's kings failed, which is why the type points beyond itself.

typology.type: Exiles seeking the welfare of Babylon, Jeremiah 29:4-7
typology.fulfillment: Jeremiah told the people deported to Babylon to build houses, plant gardens, and seek the prosperity of the city, praying for it. It is a pattern of life under a foreign power, loyal without being assimilated. Peter calls the church 'foreigners and exiles', 1 Peter 2:11, and Paul tells believers to honour the authorities, Romans 13:7. In Christ, the exiles' true citizenship is in heaven, Philippians 3:20. The type falls short because Israel's exile was a judgment and had an end date in this world; the church's exile is a mission and ends only when the King returns.

typology.type: The sword and the king's judgment, Psalm 72 and Revelation 19
typology.fulfillment: The royal Psalm 72 prays that the king would defend the afflicted and crush the oppressor. The ruler's sword in Romans 13 is a modest and partial form of that work. In Christ the sword is no longer an iron blade: the sword comes from His mouth, Revelation 19:15, and His judgment is perfect where the state's is flawed. The earthly sword is a temporary and imperfect witness to the final justice He will bring, and its limits are the reason the church longs for His appearing.

study.christ:
Authority in Romans 13 is derived, and its source is the Son. Paul says elsewhere that all things were created through Him and for Him, 'whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities', Colossians 1:16, and that He is the head over every ruler and authority, Colossians 2:10. At His resurrection He was given all authority in heaven and on earth, Matthew 28:18, and in Revelation He is 'the ruler of the kings of the earth', Revelation 1:5. The governor with a sword in Rome is one of His subjects, whether or not he knows it.

Christ's own conduct under authority sets the pattern. He paid the temple tax so as not to cause offence, though as the Son He was free, Matthew 17:24-27, He told His questioners to give to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's, Matthew 22:21, and He stood before Pilate with a calm that astonished the governor. When Pilate boasted of his power, Jesus said, 'You would have no authority over Me if it were not given to you from above', John 19:11. He did not resist the arrest with force, and He submitted to an unjust verdict. The apostle's teaching on submission is no abstraction: it is the posture of the One who was condemned by the very authority He had appointed.

Christ also exposes the limits of the state. Romans 13 says the ruler punishes wrongdoing, but at the cross the supreme judge of the age condemned the only perfectly innocent person, showing that human authority can invert justice. Yet God used that act for the salvation of the world, Acts 2:23, and the resurrection reversed the verdict. This is why Paul can call for submission and still hold that the final judgment does not belong to Caesar.

Finally Christ is the one before whom every ruler will stand. 'Every knee will bow', Philippians 2:10, and the 'kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ', Revelation 11:15. Romans 13 pictures an interim arrangement: government restraining evil until the King comes to do it perfectly.

One caution: it would be wrong to say that the passage is about Christ simply because He is mentioned, or to use Jesus' silence on politics as a licence for any regime. The link is the structure of authority that the New Testament sets out, with Christ as its source and its goal.
study.god:
The doctrine of God that the passage holds is the sovereignty of God over human governments. The sentence 'there is no authority except that which is from God' is among the most radical claims in the Bible about politics. It leaves no sphere outside His rule. Governments exist because God appointed them; they are not accidents of history or products of human will alone. Daniel 2:21 says He removes kings and establishes them, and the Lord is not surprised by any throne.

It also shows God as a God of order. The root tasso, to arrange, runs through the passage, and it is the same God who ordered creation and who is not 'a God of disorder but of peace', 1 Corinthians 14:33. He has built restraints on evil into the structure of society. In a fallen world, the ruler, the judge and the police officer are, whatever their own intentions, a mercy, because they restrain the violence that would otherwise destroy the weak.

The passage holds the justice of God and the patience of God together. The sword says that wrongdoing meets a consequence. The call to submit instead of avenge says that God has not ordained that every wrong be settled by private hands. His full verdict is yet to come, but in the meantime He gives a provisional justice. The state is a pale, partial, and sometimes corrupt echo of the justice of the Judge of all the earth, Genesis 18:25.

A real tension lies in the fact that God uses rulers who are themselves sinners. Paul does not hide it. The book of Habakkuk wrestles with the same issue, asking how a holy God can use a wicked nation, Habakkuk 1:12-13, and the answer is that God's rule is bigger than any ruler's intentions. He can use a Pharaoh and a Pilate while judging them for their own acts. This preserves both His sovereignty and the guilt of those who do evil.

For worship, the passage shapes prayer, as 1 Timothy 2:1-2 makes explicit: the church prays for those in authority, because the God who appoints them hears. It also shapes allegiance. Because God alone is God, the believer's submission to the state is real but conditional, and ultimate worship is reserved for the Lord. The one who says 'Jesus is Lord' has relativised Caesar.

crossReferences.note: Peter's parallel passage tells believers to submit to the king and to governors, who are sent to punish those who do wrong and praise those who do right. It ends 'Fear God, honour the king'. The order is deliberate: honour for the ruler, fear for God alone.

Believers are to submit to rulers, be obedient, be ready for every good work, speak evil of no one and show gentleness to all. It shows that submission to authority is part of a wider habit of public goodwill and was a settled part of Paul's teaching to young churches.

The church is to pray for kings and all in authority so that believers may lead quiet and godly lives. It turns Romans 13 from a rule of conduct into a practice of intercession and shows that the state is to be prayed for, not merely tolerated.

He changes the times and seasons, removes kings and establishes them. It is spoken in praise by a captive in Babylon, and it gives the Old Testament ground for Paul's claim that no authority exists except from God. Daniel serves a foreign king without worshipping him.

The three friends refuse to bow to the golden image and accept the furnace rather than deny God. It is the limit case that stands beside Romans 13, showing that obedience to the state stops at the point where it would require idolatry.

Peter and the apostles tell the council they must obey God rather than men. They do not riot or flee; they accept the penalty. The passage shows how disciples hold submission and conscientious refusal together.

Asked whether to pay the tax to Caesar, Jesus asks whose image is on the coin and answers that Caesar gets what is Caesar's and God what is God's. It is the root of Paul's 'pay everyone what you owe him', and it affirms two spheres without making them equals.

Pilate boasts of his power to release or crucify, and Jesus replies that he would have no authority unless it were given from above. It is the nearest Gospel statement to Romans 13:1, spoken by the one who stood before an unjust judge.

Exiles in Babylon are told to settle, build, plant, and seek the welfare of the city. The word to people under a pagan power is not escape or rebellion but prayer and work for the good of the place, which is the pattern Paul gives the Roman church.

The beast from the sea is given authority and demands worship and wages war on the saints. Set beside Romans 13, it shows what happens when the state takes God's place: the servant becomes a persecutor, and the church's call is endurance and faithfulness.

study.oneStory:
After the flood God told Noah that whoever sheds human blood will have his own blood shed by human hands, Genesis 9:5-6, which is the first sign that the human community would be given a means of restraining violence. Before it, Cain's murder and Lamech's boasting had shown what unchecked vengeance looks like. The state, in the biblical story, is not part of the original creation but a response to the fall: a common-grace provision by which God preserves a world in which evil would otherwise run unhindered.

The same story shows how rulers fail. Pharaoh enslaved Israel, Babylon destroyed Jerusalem, and Herod murdered children. Scripture tells of one nation after another that claimed more than its share, from Babel's tower to the empires of Daniel's dreams. At the same time, God raised up Joseph in Egypt, Esther in Persia, and Daniel in Babylon, and called His people to seek the good of the places where they lived.

Romans 13 sits in the stretch between the cross and the return. The King has been enthroned but not yet manifested, so the church lives under governments that are both His servants and His rivals. Paul tells it to submit, pay and honour, without surrendering the one thing that cannot be given away.

The Bible's final chapters resolve the tension. Revelation shows the empires gathered against the Lamb, Revelation 17:14, and their defeat, and then 'the kings of the earth' bringing their glory into the new Jerusalem, Revelation 21:24. The authority of earthly kings is neither erased nor left standing in its own right; it is redeemed and handed to the true King. In the new creation there will be no sword, because there will be no wrongdoer, and the nations will walk by His light. The government that Romans 13 describes will no longer be needed, and the One it served will reign for ever, Revelation 11:15.

quiz.q: Where does governing authority come from, according to Paul?

options.text: From God, who institutes the authorities that exist.
options.note: Paul says there is no authority except that which is from God.

options.text: From the consent of the people alone.
options.note: However rulers arise, Paul roots their authority ultimately in God.

options.text: From the raw power of whoever seizes control.
options.note: Authority is not mere power grabbing; it is instituted by God.

options.text: From nowhere; it is purely a human invention.
options.note: Paul explicitly grounds authority in God's appointment.

quiz.q: How does Paul describe the civil ruler in verse 4?

options.text: As God's servant for our good and an agent of retribution against wrong.
options.note: The ruler is God's diakonos, not bearing the sword in vain.

options.text: As an enemy the church should always resist.
options.note: Paul calls the ruler God's servant for good, not an enemy to resist.

options.text: As a purely neutral figure with no relation to God.
options.note: Far from neutral, the ruler is called God's servant.

options.text: As a private individual with no public duty.
options.note: The ruler holds a God-given public office for the common good.

quiz.q: Why should believers submit, according to verse 5?

options.text: Not only to avoid punishment, but also as a matter of conscience.
options.note: Submission is a matter of conscience before God, not mere fear.

options.text: Only out of fear of being punished.
options.note: Fear of punishment is real, but Paul adds the deeper reason of conscience.

options.text: Only when the ruler happens to be righteous.
options.note: Paul grounds submission in God's institution, not the ruler's private virtue.

options.text: Never; conscience forbids all submission.
options.note: Paul commands submission as a matter of conscience, not against it.

quiz.q: What does Paul say believers owe the authorities in verse 7?

options.text: Taxes, revenue, respect, and honor, each to whom it is due.
options.note: Paul lists the concrete debts of the citizen to the state.

options.text: Nothing at all, since believers are free in Christ.
options.note: Paul explicitly commands paying what is owed.

options.text: Only religious devotion, never taxes.
options.note: Paul names taxes and revenue specifically, not only inward attitudes.

options.text: Complete worship as to God Himself.
options.note: Worship belongs to God alone; the state receives honor and dues, not worship.

quiz.q: How does this passage relate to the higher allegiance owed to God?

options.text: Authority is real but derived from God, so we obey God above all when they conflict.
options.note: The orthodox reading: submit to the state, yet obey God rather than men when commanded to sin.

options.text: It demands unconditional obedience to rulers in absolutely everything.
options.note: Scripture as a whole limits obedience: we must obey God rather than men.

options.text: It teaches that the state may be freely ignored whenever inconvenient.
options.note: Paul commands genuine submission, not casual disregard.

options.text: It says the state has no relation to God at all.
options.note: The state is precisely God's servant, derived from and accountable to Him.

questions: Paul roots all authority in God's appointment. How does seeing government as part of God's ordering of the world shape the way you think and speak about those who govern?
Submission is to flow from conscience, not merely fear of punishment. Where might God be calling you to a more honest, conscientious citizenship?
The ruler is called God's servant for good. How can you pray for and honor those in authority even when you disagree with them?
Paul places the state's sword right after forbidding personal revenge. How does trusting God's ordained justice free you from taking matters into your own hands?
Our highest allegiance is always to God. How do you discern the difference between lawful submission to authority and the point where you must obey God rather than men?

translationNotes.note: Governing authorities renders a phrase for the ruling powers; Paul's point is that all legitimate authority is derived, there is none except from God, which both dignifies and limits every human office.

He does not carry the sword in vain speaks of the state's God-given judicial power to punish wrongdoing, the appointed alternative to the personal vengeance forbidden in 12:19; agent of retribution renders a word for one who executes wrath.
God's servants here renders leitourgoi, a term for public or even priestly ministers, dignifying civic office as service under God and grounding the duty to pay taxes in His ordering of society.
